doc.title: Joe Wilder Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 12, 1998

title: Learning small-group playing in Lonnie Slappey's band
summary: Wilder learned combo playing by doing it in Philadelphia, taking Frank Galbraith's place in Lonnie Slappey's John Kirby-style group while still in school.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Now you got a bachelor’s from Manhattan School of Music.
The process of learning how to function in a combo for instance, the jazz etiquette and so forth, did you get any of that there or how do you learn that?
You mean going from the jazz to the classical?
Yes. I mean how did you learn to play in a small combo? Was it simply by doing it?

Basically that’s what it was, yeah. In Philadelphia I played with a small group, Lonnie Slappey’s band, and there was a trumpet player, Frank Galbraith, who was really an exceptional — he had a different style from almost anybody else that I had heard. And he sort of established the style of this group. But it was predicated more or less on the John Kirby Band, because the make-up of the band was basically the same. But it was a different style band. And I took his place, and I was still in school at the time. So from listening to him and the things he did, I began trying to do some things of mine that were not necessarily anywhere near the kinds of things he did, but I would get an opportunity to experiment, and some things worked and those things I retained, and the others I let go, but it was a chance for me to practice all the time and get that experience. It’s a little different playing in a small group. It’s like playing in a brass quintet and chamber orchestras you know. There’s more exposed playing. It calls for a little more technique very often because you’re not buried in a section with an orchestra of 60 or 70 people or something like that. And everything you do someone can focus on so you develop a little more technique and more daring.
Is it harder for the trumpet player to play in quintets and sextets because the trumpet man usually is responsible for the melody?

They are. But everyone is sort of — this is where you’re more or less, everyone is treated equally by the composers and the music you’re playing. Because in quintets, regardless of what chair you’re playing, your chair is very important. And at some point you’re playing solo, you’re playing solo parts. It’s very interesting, and you develop a sense of relationship musically to the other players you’re playing with in the group. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -14-
